extracted.intended_audience: social scientists, historians, philosophers of science, and advanced students of methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the correct method for deriving generalizations in social science from history and human nature, distinguishing empirical laws from scientific theorems and prescribing how to verify and connect them. Emphasizes social statics vs dynamics and the requisites of stable political society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not introduce historical generalizations without grounding in human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an imperative rule never to introduce any generalization from history into the social science unless sufficient grounds can be pointed out for it in human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A generalization traceable in historical succession can only be an empirical law unless it is connected with psychological and ethological laws and converted, by the consilience of deduction a priori with historical evidence, into a scientific law. Empirical historical regularities alone are insufficient for reliable prediction beyond adjacent cases. (Mentions M. Comte as an example of seeing this necessity.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Constantly verify empirical laws by psychological and ethological laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws of society require constant verification by the laws of human nature (psychological and ethological laws).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The only effective corrective against erroneous generalizations from history is continual checking against the principles of human nature; without such verification, historical generalizations are likely to be wrong. This verification is indispensable even where historical instances suggest a derivative law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require competent investigators versed in human nature laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Only persons competently skilled in psychological and ethological laws are capable of preparing the materials for historical generalization or of judging which facts are comparatively important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unskilled observers will fail to know what facts to look for or how to estimate evidential marks that must be inferred rather than directly observed. Competence is required to analyze historical facts and to avoid spurious generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between Social Statics (co-existence) and Social Dynamics (succession)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws of society are of two kinds: uniformities of co-existence (Social Statics) and uniformities of succession (Social Dynamics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social Statics studies conditions of stability and the mutual relations of contemporaneous social phenomena (analogy to anatomy/organization), while Social Dynamics studies laws of progress and the sequences of social conditions (analogy to mechanics/life). Each branch has distinct aims and methods and both are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: In Social Statics, analyze social elements relatively by their interdependence
rubrics_metrics.description: When using the statical view, each social element must be considered always and exclusively in relation to all the other elements, to infer characteristic marks of distinct modes of social existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This relational method allows inferring the state of some elements from others previously known (useful where direct observation is impracticable). It is analogous to inferring bodily conditions in anatomy from related structures. Use caution: the relations are complex and indirect inference requires careful estimation of limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate limits of variation; avoid oversimple coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Necessary relations among aspects of the same social organism cannot be so simple and precise that observed results could only have arisen from one mode of coordination; one must estimate the limits of variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to estimate these limits (both healthy and morbid) may make indirect exploration lead into error. The exact estimation of limits of variation complements sociological statics to prevent false inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine statical and dynamical views to derive correspondence laws
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain better empirical laws, combine the statical view of contemporaneous conditions with the dynamical view of progressive changes, so as to empirically obtain laws of correspondence between simultaneous states and simultaneous changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This law of correspondence, duly verified a priori, would become the derivative law of human development. Practically, one should not rest on isolated progressive observations of fragments but relate simultaneous conditions and their changes across elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and follow a pre-eminent social element (intellectual convictions) as central chain
rubrics_metrics.description: If one social element is pre-eminent as the prime agent of social movement, take its progress as the central chain around which other developments are appended; historical evidence points to the state of speculative faculties (beliefs and knowledge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The progress of knowledge limits industrial and artistic improvement; changes in prevalent beliefs commonly precede large social changes. Use the progress of intellectual convictions to order the filiation of social facts when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive empirical laws from sufficient and well-compared instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws must be based on a sufficient number and quality of historical instances; few instances, or imperfectly known cases, will likely produce erroneous generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because few nations have attained high social stages independently, empirical laws often rest on limited samples; ensure adequate comparative analysis and detailed knowledge of instances before asserting general laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert empirical laws into scientific theorems by a priori deduction plus historical verification (consilience)
rubrics_metrics.description: An empirical law attains scientific rank only when it can be connected with the laws of human nature and shown by deduction a priori to be a necessary derivative, corroborated by historical evidence (consilience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the essential methodological step: do not accept empirical generalizations as scientific without demonstrating their derivation from ultimate psychological/ethological principles and verifying them historically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek the 'axiomata media' — derivative laws that generate filiation between generations
rubrics_metrics.description: The aim of social dynamics is to ascertain the intermediate ('middle') principles or derivative laws (axiomata media) by which social states generate one another across generations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct derivation from elementary human nature laws may be impracticable because of the long series of interactions; identifying these middle principles is the feasible way to explain filiation in social progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use indirect exploration when direct observation is impracticable but note its provisional character
rubrics_metrics.description: Social statics may provisionally supply the place of direct observation by judging certain elements from their relations to others previously known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This resource is valuable (e.g., assessing alleged ancient achievements by relation to general scientific/artistic state), but its provisional nature and susceptibility to error must be acknowledged and limited by further verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate 'progress' with 'improvement'—treat progressiveness as change, not value judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The words Progress and Progressiveness are not synonymous with improvement; laws may determine a series of changes that are not necessarily improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For methodological purposes it suffices to assume progressive change in the character of successive generations; whether those changes are improvements is a separate scientific question, not an assumption for method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political-stability requisites: existence of laws, tribunals, and organized executive force
rubrics_metrics.description: No numerous society has been held together without laws (or equivalent usages), tribunals, and an organized force to execute decisions; public authorities obeyed or deemed to have a right to be obeyed are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are empirical conditions observed in all societies maintaining collective existence; their cessation leads to merging into another society or reconstitution on a new basis. Use psychological confirmation to elevate to scientific truth where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisite: System of education with restraining discipline for citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: A comprehensive system of education—beginning in infancy and continued through life—with restraining discipline is essential to train individuals to subordinate personal impulses to the ends of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education's role is to inculcate habits of subordination and self-control necessary for social order; relaxation of restraining discipline tends to internal disorganization and decline. Historical examples: ancient commonwealths and the role of religious teaching in modern nations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisite: Existence of allegiance or loyalty—a fixed point for social unity
rubrics_metrics.description: A feeling of allegiance or loyalty (attachment to some settled, secure element—gods, persons, laws, or principles) is necessary in durable political societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This stable point may attach to gods, rulers, laws, liberties, or principles (e.g., individual freedom). Its presence prevents habitual contesting of fundamental principles; its habitual absence places the polity in a state akin to civil war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisite: Principle of cohesion (sympathy and common interest among members)
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong and active principle of cohesion—sympathy, common interest, feeling of being one people—is essential; not a hostile nationalism but union and mutual concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cohesion prevents parts of the state from treating one another as foreigners and reduces secessionist tendencies. Historical illustrations include Rome's integration of provinces and modern contrasts (England/Ireland, Italy, German/Austrian empire, South American republics).
